cards.front: Define gravitational field strength and give its unit.
cards.back: The force per unit mass on a small test mass placed at that point, g = F/m, in N/kg.
cards.explanation: N/kg and m/s^2 are the same unit: the field strength at a point is numerically the acceleration of free fall there.

cards.back: Every mass attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres: F = G m1 m2 / r^2.

keyPoints.text: force proportional to the product of the masses
inversely proportional to the square of the separation

cards.explanation: The inverse-square dependence is why doubling the separation quarters the force, and r is measured between centres rather than surfaces.

cards.front: Define the gravitational potential at a point, and state its sign.
cards.back: The work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to that point. It is always negative.
cards.explanation: Infinity is taken as zero potential and gravity is always attractive, so work is always released rather than needed and the potential is negative.

cards.front: Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of a planet of mass 6.0 x 10^24 kg and radius 6.4 x 10^6 m, using G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2.
cards.explanation: g = GM/r^2 = (6.67 x 10^-11 x 6.0 x 10^24) / (6.4 x 10^6)^2 = 9.8 N/kg. Forgetting to square the radius gives 6.3 x 10^7 N/kg.

cards.front: What three conditions must a geostationary orbit satisfy?
cards.back: It must be above the equator, have a period of 24 hours matching the Earth's rotation, and travel in the same direction as the Earth spins, so the satellite stays above one point on the surface.

synonyms: same period as the Earth's rotation

keyPoints.text: same direction as the Earth's rotation
stays above the same point on the surface

cards.explanation: An inclined orbit would make the satellite drift north and south each day, so only an equatorial orbit can appear stationary.
